questions.q: Which part of an uploaded file can your server actually verify?
questions.explain: The name, the declared type and any size header are written by the client, and an attacker writes whatever gets past you. The bytes are what you store, so you check those.
options: The file name, because the browser sets it
The part's Content-Type, because the browser sets it from the extension
The bytes: their length, and their first bytes, which reveal the real format
Nothing; uploads cannot be checked

questions.q: A handler saves uploads with writeFile(join("uploads", file.filename), bytes). What can a client do with the file name ../../app/config.json?
questions.explain: join resolves .., which is exactly what climbs out of the folder. Never use a client's name as a path; generate the key and keep the cleaned name as a label.
options: Nothing, join removes .. parts
Write outside uploads/, possibly overwriting the server's own files (path traversal)
Only create a folder called ..
Make the upload fail with a 400

questions.q: Which object key is the best choice for an attachment of task 12?
questions.explain: A generated random key contains nothing the user typed, cannot collide, cannot be guessed, and the tasks/12/ prefix still lets you list a task's files. A timestamp can collide and is guessable; an email in a key leaks personal data into logs and URLs.
options: tasks/12/${file.filename}
${file.filename}
tasks/12/${randomUUID()}, with the cleaned file name stored in the database
tasks/12/${Date.now()}
uploads/${userEmail}/${file.filename}

questions.q: What does extractBoundary return for these two headers?
questions.explain: The boundary is the string that separates the parts of a multipart body, named in the Content-Type. A JSON request has none, which is why the route answers 415 instead of trying to parse it.
options: ----zudo42 undefined
----zudo42 null
boundary=----zudo42 undefined
zudo42 undefined

questions.q: A browser on Windows sends this form. What does the parser give you?
questions.explain: Text parts become fields, file parts become files. The parser reduces the file name to a safe base name, so the Windows path is gone. The size is the 8 bytes of %PDF-1.7; the line break before the next boundary belongs to the format, not the file.
options: receipt [ [ 'file', 'scan.pdf', 'application/pdf', 8 ] ]
receipt [ [ 'file', 'C:\\Users\\ada\\scan.pdf', 'application/pdf', 8 ] ]
undefined [ [ 'file', 'scan.pdf', 'application/pdf', 8 ] ]
receipt [ [ 'file', 'scan.pdf', 'application/pdf', 10 ] ]

questions.q: What happens when a form has more fields than allowed?
questions.explain: Every parser limit (file size, number of files, fields, field size) throws a MultipartLimitError with status 413. A form with 100,000 tiny fields is also a way to exhaust a server.
options: MultipartLimitError 413 Maximum number of multipart fields exceeded.
MultipartParseError 400 Maximum number of multipart fields exceeded.
HttpError 400 Too many fields
nothing is printed; extra fields are dropped

questions.q: Why must maxBodySize on the node adapter be set for an upload API, even though the multipart parser has maxFileSize?
questions.explain: Limits only help if they act before the work they limit. The parser runs inside your handler, after the body has been read. The adapter's limit is the first gate, and it answers 413 on its own.
options: The parser ignores maxFileSize
The adapter reads the whole body into memory before any route runs; only its limit stops a huge request before the bytes are in memory
maxBodySize sets the per-file limit
It does not matter; either limit alone is enough

questions.q: Your API accepts up to 3 files of 2 MB each in one request, and JSON bodies elsewhere. What is a sensible maxBodySize?
questions.explain: maxBodySize applies to every route, so choose the largest real request and no more. Anything much bigger than a few megabytes should go directly to object storage with a presigned URL instead.
options: Unlimited, to be safe for uploads
2 MB, the size of one file
A little over 6 MB (say 7 MB), the largest legitimate request plus the multipart overhead
1 GB, in case users upload videos later

questions.q: Match the failure to its status: the body is 8 MB over the limit; the file is empty; the bytes are HTML but the part says image/png.
questions.explain: 413 Payload Too Large for size, 400 Bad Request for a malformed or empty file, and 415 Unsupported Media Type for a type you do not accept. Distinct codes let a client show the right message.

questions.q: What is a "magic number" in a file?
questions.explain: Most binary formats begin with a fixed signature. Reading it to decide the real type is content sniffing, and it is far harder to fake by accident than an extension or a header.
options: A checksum at the end of the file
A fixed sequence of bytes at the start of a file that identifies its format, like %PDF- for PDF
The file's size, stored in its header
A random number the browser adds to each upload

questions.q: What does this sniffer print?
questions.explain: %PDF- is exactly the PDF signature. The SVG matches nothing on the allow-list. The last file is too short: bytes[3] is undefined, not 0x47, so a truncated PNG signature does not count.
options:
application/pdf
unknown
unknown

application/pdf
image/svg+xml
image/png

application/pdf
unknown
image/png

unknown
unknown
unknown

questions.q: Why should SVG not be on an image allow-list that is served from your main domain?
questions.explain: Some "images" are documents that can run code. If you must accept SVG, convert it to PNG on upload or serve it from a separate domain.
options: SVG files are always very large
Browsers cannot display SVG
SVG is XML and can contain <script>; opened from your domain it runs like a page (stored XSS)
SVG has no magic number, so it cannot be uploaded

questions.q: A part declares image/jpeg and its bytes start with the PNG signature. Both types are allowed. What does the lesson's checkFile do, and why?
questions.explain: An honest browser gets this right. A mismatch usually means a renamed file or a probe, and refusing it costs a legitimate user very little. application/octet-stream means "I don't know", so it defers to the sniffed type.
options: Accept it as a JPEG, because the client said so
Accept it as a PNG silently
Refuse it with 415: a file whose claim contradicts its content is suspicious, unless the claim is the generic application/octet-stream
Convert it to JPEG

questions.q: The lesson's policy renames files so the extension matches the sniffed type. What names does this print?
questions.explain: Only the last extension is replaced, so the name always ends in the real type and nobody downloads an "exe". A name that is only an extension becomes empty after the replace, and the || "file" fallback gives it a name.
options:
invoice.pdf.pdf
holiday.jpg
file.png

invoice.pdf
holiday.jpg
.png

invoice.pdf.exe.pdf
holiday.jpg
.png.png

invoice.pdf.pdf
holiday
file.png

questions.q: What does sanitizeFilename from @zudojs/http make of these names? (A generated name is shown as upload-….)
questions.explain: It keeps only the base name, drops control characters such as the NUL byte, and replaces a name with nothing usable left (like ..) by a generated one. Even so, the lesson uses the result only as a label, never as a storage path.
options: [ 'report.pdf', 'passwd', 'c.png', 'upload-…', 'xy.png' ]
[ 'report.pdf', 'etc/passwd', 'a/b/c.png', '..', 'x y.png' ]
[ 'report.pdf', '..-..-etc-passwd', 'a-b-c.png', 'upload-…', 'xy.png' ]
[ 'report.pdf', 'passwd', 'c.png', '', 'x' ]

questions.q: Saving an attachment writes the bytes to object storage and a row to the database. They cannot share a transaction. Which order does the lesson use, and why?
questions.explain: A row without bytes is a broken link users can click. Bytes without a row are invisible and can be cleaned up by a sweeper. Choose the order whose failure is harmless.
options: Row first, so the user sees the file sooner
Bytes first, then the row, deleting the bytes if the row fails: the worst leftover is an invisible orphan, never a row pointing at a missing file
Both at the same time with Promise.all
It does not matter

questions.q: This service stores, then records, and compensates on failure. What is printed?
questions.explain: The second object was stored, the insert failed on the foreign key, and the catch deleted the object before passing the error on. One object, one row. The deletion is called a compensating action.
options:
failed: 23503
[ 'tasks/1/a' ] 1

failed: 23503
[ 'tasks/1/a', 'tasks/9/b' ] 1
[ 'tasks/1/a' ] 1

failed: 23503
[ 'tasks/1/a', 'tasks/9/b' ] 2

questions.q: A request carries three files, and the third is not an allowed type. Why does uploadAll run checkFile on every file before storing any?
questions.explain: Validate everything that can be validated up front. Failures that can only happen while storing (storage down) are then handled by removing the files already saved.
options: Checking is faster in a batch
So a bad file is refused before anything is stored, and the request fails as a whole instead of leaving the first two behind
Because storage can only take one file per request
So the files are stored in alphabetical order

questions.q: Why does the service rely on the foreign key on attachments.task_id to answer 404 for a missing task, instead of only checking "does the task exist?" first?
questions.explain: "Check, then act" has a gap. A pre-check can still be useful to avoid storing bytes you will delete, but the constraint is what makes the rule hold.
options: Foreign keys are faster than a SELECT
The task can be deleted between the check and the insert; the foreign key is the only check that is still true at the moment of the write
A SELECT cannot return a 404
The storage package requires it

questions.q: What does the response header X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff do for a download?
questions.explain: Without it, some browsers "help" by rendering content that looks like HTML as HTML, which turns an uploaded file into a page on your domain. Saving instead of opening is Content-Disposition: attachment's job.
options: It stops the file from being cached
It tells the browser to use the Content-Type you sent and not guess another type from the content, for example HTML
It encrypts the download
It forces the browser to save the file

questions.q: Why build the Content-Disposition header with createAttachmentDisposition(name) instead of `attachment; filename="${name}"`?
questions.explain: File names are user input, and headers have their own syntax. Set-Cookie smuggled through a file name is a real attack. Let the helper do the quoting and the filename* encoding.
options: The template string is slower
A name with a quote or a line break could end the header and start a new one (response splitting); the helper escapes quotes, drops control characters and encodes non-ASCII names
Browsers ignore hand-written headers
The helper also compresses the file

questions.q: Why does the download route send Cache-Control: private?
questions.explain: private allows the user's own browser to cache the response but forbids shared caches. Attachments usually belong to a person or a team.
options: So the browser never caches the file
So shared caches such as a company proxy or a CDN do not store one user's private file and serve it to someone else
It is required for PDF files
So the download is faster

questions.q: A lock expires while its holder is still busy. What does this print?
questions.explain: The first lock expired after 20 ms, so the second was granted with a bigger fence. The first holder may not know it lost the lock: that is why the resource has to check the fence.
options: 1 2 false true
1 1 false true
1 2 true true
nothing is printed; the second acquire waits forever

questions.q: Where must the fence check happen for it to stop a stale write?
questions.explain: isHeld() can be true at the check and false a millisecond later, during a pause. Only the resource sees every write in order, so only it can refuse the one carrying an older token.
options: In the service, before calling the database: if (lock.isHeld())
In the lock manager, when the lock is released
In the protected resource, in the same step as the write, for example UPDATE … WHERE cover_fence < $fence
In the client, before it sends the request

questions.q: A store that remembers the highest fence receives these writes. What is printed?
questions.explain: Fence 2 arrived after fence 3: its holder's lock had already passed to someone else. Refusing it keeps the newer cover. The order of arrival does not matter; the order of the fences does.
options:
saved draft.png
saved final.png
refused stale.png (fence 2 <= 3)
final.png

saved draft.png
saved final.png
saved stale.png
stale.png

saved draft.png
refused final.png (fence 3 <= 1)
saved stale.png
stale.png

saved draft.png
saved final.png
refused stale.png (fence 2 <= 3)
stale.png

questions.q: You run the Task API on three servers, each with its own InMemoryLockManager. What happens to cover replacements?
questions.explain: An in-memory lock only coordinates code in one process. The database's fence check stays the same, but the fence numbers must come from something all servers share.
options: They are still safe, because each server has a lock
Each server hands out its own locks and fences, so two servers can both hold "the" lock with fence 1; you need a shared lock or fence source (PostgreSQL, Redis)
The servers share memory automatically
Only the first server can accept uploads

questions.q: Which situation leaves an orphaned object that compensation cannot clean up?
questions.explain: Compensation is code that runs after an error your code sees. A crash or a failing delete leaves bytes nobody references. A sweeper finds and removes them later.
options: The database refuses the row with a foreign key error
The file is the wrong type
The process is killed after put and before the INSERT, or the compensating delete itself fails
The client cancels the request before sending the body

questions.q: Why does the orphan sweeper only delete objects older than a grace period?
questions.explain: The grace period must be longer than any upload can take between the two writes. Anything younger might still be in progress.
options: Old objects are bigger
An upload that is between its put and its INSERT right now also looks like an orphan; deleting it would break a successful upload
Object storage cannot delete new objects
To save money on list requests

questions.q: The sweeper compares stored objects with referenced keys, with a 60-minute grace period. What does it delete?
questions.explain: b is old and unreferenced: an orphan. c is unreferenced but only 5 minutes old, so it may be an upload in progress. a and d are referenced.
options: [ 'tasks/1/b' ]
[ 'tasks/1/b', 'tasks/2/c' ]
[ 'tasks/2/c' ]
[ 'tasks/1/b', 'tasks/2/d' ]

questions.q: When deleting an attachment, the service deletes the database row first and the object second. Why that order?
questions.explain: It is the same rule as for uploads, mirrored: always choose the order whose half-finished state is invisible to users.
options: Rows are faster to delete
If the second step fails, the leftover is an unreferenced object (swept later), not a row pointing at a deleted file
Object storage refuses deletes of referenced objects
The order does not matter for deletes

questions.q: How does the lesson test that a failure in the second storage write leaves nothing behind?
questions.explain: ObjectStorage is an interface, so a test can put a failing implementation in its place. Fault injection makes rare failures happen on demand, which is the only way to test recovery code.
options: By unplugging the disk during the test
By mocking the whole service
By wrapping the real ObjectStorage in one that throws on the second put, then checking that no objects and no rows remain
By waiting for a real failure in production

questions.q: Users need to upload 500 MB videos. What is the usual design?
questions.explain: Large files should not pass through your API process's memory at all. A presigned URL allows exactly one upload of one key for a short time, and the API still checks size and type before trusting it.
options: Raise maxBodySize to 1 GB
Base64-encode the video into a JSON body
The API signs a short-lived presigned URL; the client uploads straight to object storage, then tells the API, which checks the object before recording it
Split the video into 2 MB attachments

questions.q: Object storage keeps some metadata with each object (content type, { taskId: "1" }). What is the source of truth for which files a task has?
questions.explain: One place must be the truth. The database can be queried, joined and constrained; object metadata is a helpful label, for example when a sweeper or an engineer looks at an unknown object.
options: The attachments table: it is what the API lists, checks permissions against and deletes from; object metadata helps when inspecting storage by hand
The object metadata, because it travels with the bytes
The file names in the storage folder
The browser's cache

questions.q: Finish sniff(bytes). Return "image/png" when the bytes start with 89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A, "image/jpeg" when they start with FF D8 FF, and null otherwise.
questions.explain: Compare the first bytes with each signature. Reading past the end of a short array gives undefined, which never equals a byte, so a truncated signature is refused without a separate length check.

questions.q: Finish attachmentKey(taskId, id). Throw a RangeError("taskId must be a positive whole number") unless taskId is a safe integer of at least 1; otherwise return tasks/<taskId>/<id>. The file name must play no part.
questions.explain: Number.isSafeInteger is false for strings, fractions and NaN, so one check covers them all. In the real service the id is randomUUID(), and the key never contains anything the user typed.
questions.expected:
tasks/12/7f3a
0 -> taskId must be a positive whole number
1.5 -> taskId must be a positive whole number
12 -> taskId must be a positive whole number
NaN -> taskId must be a positive whole number

questions.q: Finish check(file) for PDFs only. Return "400 empty" for no bytes, "413 too large" for more than 1000 bytes, "415 not a pdf" when the bytes do not start with %PDF-, and "ok" otherwise. Check in that order.
questions.explain: Cheap checks first: length costs nothing, and refusing a huge file before looking at it avoids work. Only the first five bytes are decoded, never the whole file.
questions.expected:
ok
400 empty
413 too large
415 not a pdf

questions.q: Finish uploadAll(files). Store each file with save(file), which returns an id or throws. If one throws, call remove(id) for every file already saved, then rethrow. Return the list of ids on success.
questions.explain: Files 3 and 4 were saved, then the third file failed, and both were removed again: the request succeeded or failed as a whole. The earlier, successful request was not touched.

questions.q: Finish setCover(task, key, fence) for an in-memory task row { coverKey, coverFence }. If fence is not greater than task.coverFence, return { ok: false } and change nothing. Otherwise store the key and the fence and return { ok: true, oldKey } with the key it replaced.
questions.explain: This is what the lesson's UPDATE … WHERE cover_fence < $2 RETURNING old.old_key does in one statement. The caller deletes oldKey after a success, and deletes its own new object after a refusal.

questions.q: Finish findOrphans(objects, referenced, graceMs, now). Return the keys of objects that are not in the referenced set and are older than graceMs (now - lastModified > graceMs), in the order given.
questions.explain: With a 10-minute grace, nothing is old enough to delete, even though nothing is referenced. Passing now in, instead of calling Date.now() inside, is what makes the function easy to test.

questions.q: Finish downloadHeaders(row). Return an object with content-type set to row.contentType, x-content-type-options set to nosniff, cache-control set to private, max-age=0, and content-disposition set to attachment; filename="…" where the name has every character other than letters, digits, dot, dash, underscore and space replaced by _.
questions.explain: An allow-list of characters is the simplest safe rule: the quote and the line break become _, so the header cannot be split. In the real server, createAttachmentDisposition does this and also keeps non-ASCII names readable with filename*.
